lesson.menu_title: What Would You Do? — The Memo Nobody Asked For
lesson.menu_desc: The second conditional, for the ideas you have never said out loud at work -- 37 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 6 -- What Would You Do?
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Rosa M. Mitiko Shida | Lesson 6 -- What Would You Do?

listenings.text: Rosa, it is Beatriz from the regional director's office. He is preparing the strategy session for December and he has asked four account managers for something unusual. Not a report. One page, informal, answering a single question: what would you change if the decision were yours? He is serious about the informal part. He said, and I am quoting him, that if he wanted a formal document he would ask the consultants, and that he already knows what the consultants would say. He wants the version you would tell a colleague in the corridor. One page, by the end of the month. And if you would rather talk it through instead of writing it, call me and we will book twenty minutes with him.

Here is the thing about strategy that nobody says out loud in the meeting. Most people in this industry know exactly what they would change. Ask any account manager what they would do if they ran the commercial area, and you will get a clear, specific, sensible answer in about fifteen seconds. Ask the same person to write it in a document that goes upstairs and it takes three weeks and comes back as nothing. The problem is not the idea. The problem is that we treat the strategy conversation as if it needed a special language. It does not. If I could change one thing about how this company plans, I would ask people the question in the corridor and write down what they actually say.

reading.rtitle: The Best Idea in the Room Never Reaches the Room
paras: Every large company has the same quiet problem. The person who knows most about a client is almost never the person who decides what happens to that client, and the distance between the two is measured in documents.

If you asked an account manager what she would change about the commercial strategy, she would tell you in one minute. She talks to those clients every week. She knows which contract is at risk, which competitor is calling them, and which of our own processes is costing us the renewal. If she ran the area, she would fix three things, and she could name them without preparing.

Now ask her to put it in writing for the board. Something changes. The one-minute answer becomes a document with an executive summary, and by the third version the three specific things have turned into general statements about excellence and alignment. Nobody lied. The idea simply did not survive the format.

The companies that get this right do something almost embarrassingly simple. They ask the question in the corridor, in ordinary language, and they write down the answer as it was said. If more organizations did that, they would find that the strategy they are paying consultants to discover is already sitting in the heads of the people who answer the phone on a Friday evening.
reading.source: Column -- South America Commercial Aviation Review

gist.prompt: What is this column mainly about?
choices: Why account managers should be promoted to the board
Why good ideas get lost between the corridor and the formal document
How to write a better executive summary

items: The column says account managers do not know what they would change.
If you asked an account manager what she would change, she would tell you in one minute.
The problem, according to the column, is the format and not the idea.
Nobody lied. The idea simply did not survive the format.
The column suggests hiring more consultants to find the strategy.
The strategy they are paying consultants to discover is already sitting in the heads of the people who answer the phone.
The solution proposed is to ask the question in ordinary language and record the answer.
They ask the question in the corridor, in ordinary language, and they write down the answer as it was said.

items.situation: The regional director asks, informally: what would you change if the decision were yours?
tips: If plus past simple, then would plus the base verb
Name one specific thing, not three general ones

items.situation: A colleague asks how you would handle a client who is talking to a competitor.
tips: I would call them before the renewal, not after
Say what you would do first, then why

items.situation: Somebody proposes cutting the team to save money.
tips: Push back with a hypothetical, not with a complaint
If we cut two people, we would lose the two biggest accounts

items.situation: You are asked what you would need in order to take on the Chile accounts.
tips: Name the condition as a hypothetical
If I had one more analyst, I would take them tomorrow

items.situation: A client asks what you would do in his position.
tips: If I were you is the fixed form -- not if I was you

items.situation: The director asks why nobody has said this before.
tips: Because if we wrote it down, it would stop sounding like this

extra_audio.text: Diego says the regional director has asked him for one informal page about what he would change. Rosa answers that she received the same request and that the informal part is the difficult part. Diego explains the one thing he would change if the decision were his. Rosa says that in his position she would start with the renewal process instead. The two of them agree to read each other's page before the end of the month.
